chosen_title: Geoengineering could expose plane passengers to sulphuric acid
caption:
The plan to cool Earth could turn every polar flight path into a chemical hazard. ✈️

Scientists and policymakers are seriously exploring stratospheric aerosol injection — spraying sun-reflecting sulfate particles into the upper atmosphere near the poles — as an emergency brake on global warming. The theory is compelling: bounce enough sunlight back into space and buy the planet time while emissions are cut.

But a new analysis reported by New Scientist has exposed a dangerous blind spot. Those sulfate particles behave as sulphuric acid droplets in the cold polar stratosphere. Commercial aircraft routinely cross polar regions on high-traffic routes — London to New York, Tokyo to Vancouver, Frankfurt to Los Angeles — meaning flights would regularly pass through artificially created clouds of sulphuric acid. Researchers warn this poses a direct risk to passengers, crew, and aircraft components exposed repeatedly to the corrosive haze.

The finding arrives as geoengineering shifts from fringe science to serious policy debate, with no binding international framework yet governing who can deploy it, when, or who is liable for side effects.

Why it matters: Climate solutions at planetary scale carry planetary-scale risks — and this one could affect anyone who boards a long-haul flight.

Source: New Scientist

slides.headline: The world's most ambitious climate plan has a terrifying blind spot

slides.label: THE STORY
slides.headline: A Climate Fix With a Hidden Catch
slides.body: Scientists have proposed fighting global warming by spraying sun-reflecting sulfate particles into the stratosphere near the Earth's poles — a technique called polar stratospheric aerosol injection. The idea is to bounce sunlight back into space before it heats the planet. But a new study reported by New Scientist reveals a serious problem nobody fully mapped: commercial aircraft flying through these artificially created particle clouds would be exposed to sulphuric acid, putting passengers and crew at direct risk.

slides.label: HOW IT WORKS
slides.art_prompt: A side-on cartoon cutaway of the Earth's polar stratosphere: tiny scientists on a research vessel fire silver particles from a cannon into a high atmospheric layer, where the particles form a shimmering reflective haze that bounces yellow sunlight arrows back into space. Just below the haze layer, a commercial jumbo jet flies directly into the chemical cloud, the plane's fuselage already beginning to acquire a faint acidic sheen, while a flock of confused penguins watches from the ice sheet below. No text in the image.
slides.headline: Sulfate in the Sky = Acid in the Air
slides.body: Sulfate aerosols sprayed into the cold polar stratosphere behave chemically like sulphuric acid droplets. Polar flight routes connecting North America, Europe, and Asia cross directly through the zones where these particles would accumulate.

slides.headline: Your Flight, Through a Cloud of Sulphuric Acid
slides.body: Researchers warn repeated exposure to sulphuric acid clouds could corrode aircraft engines and fuselages, and potentially harm passengers and crew if contaminated air enters the cabin system.

slides.label: WHY IT MATTERS
points: Polar stratospheric aerosol injection is being seriously explored by governments and climate scientists as a last-resort tool to slow warming without requiring immediate deep emissions cuts.
Commercial polar routes — among the busiest in the world — cross exactly the regions where sulfate particles would be concentrated, making the risk global, not regional.

The discovery adds to a growing list of geoengineering side effects: other studies have flagged disrupted monsoon patterns, unequal cooling across the Northern and Southern hemispheres, and ozone depletion.
There is currently no binding international framework governing who can deploy stratospheric aerosol injection, under what conditions, or who bears legal responsibility when things go wrong.
